implementation_notes: Kotlin's 'inline' is a real keyword with a language-level purpose: it substitutes the function body at the call site, which (a) removes the call and enables non-local returns from lambdas and (b) avoids the allocation of a lambda object when the lambda is passed as an argument. That second effect is the reason Kotlin's stdlib marks withLock, let, run, apply, and use inline: a non-inline higher-order function allocates a Function object per call, and in a hot loop that allocation dominates. It also enables the crossinline/noinline modifiers to control exactly which lambdas are inlined. The cost is the same as elsewhere - code size and the loss of a single compiled body - and Kotlin's stdlib uses it precisely where a lambda is created per call (a scope function in a hot loop), not everywhere. In Kotlin/JVM the JIT would inline a small lambda's body anyway, but the point is to avoid the *allocation* of the lambda object, which the JIT cannot always eliminate.
idiom_name: inline functions (inline / crossinline / noinline modifiers) to avoid lambda allocation and enable non-local returns
pitfalls: An inline function's parameters are re-evaluated at the call site, so a parameter with side effects behaves differently than in a non-inline function.
inline allocates a Function object per call if any parameter is stored or passed on - inline only helps when the lambda is called directly.
Code size multiplies at every call site; a large inline body in a widely-used scope function bloats the binary.
An inline function cannot be virtual and cannot be a member of a class in the usual sense; inlining is decided at compile time, so it cannot be overridden.
On Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS the cost model differs from the JVM - what inlines on the JVM may not on Native.
